questions.prompt: The summary says: 'Removed -q 30 from the varcall call: it is the default in varcall 2.4.' How do you check this claim?
questions.explain: A flag default is a checkable fact. Read it from the tool's own help or docs for the version you run, which the agent did not write.

options.text: Read varcall's own help for that flag, on your version
Ask the agent whether it is sure about that default, and trust a firm yes
options.misconception: Asking the same agent often gets a fluent yes, and a fluent yes adds no independent check.

options.text: Accept it, because the agent named an exact version number and a flag
options.misconception: A precise detail adds confidence only. The tool's own help is the check.

options.text: Run the pipeline once and accept the claim if it finishes
options.misconception: A run that finishes shows the script works. It does not show which quality cutoff was applied.

questions.prompt: Transcript and summary lines, in order. Which one is destructive and has no way back?
questions.explain: rm -rf deletes at once and git cannot restore untracked results. Make the change reversible first.

lines.why: It writes a new file and removes nothing.

lines.text: Cleaned old output: rm -rf results/ && mkdir results

lines.why: Re-running is fine once its inputs are safe.

questions.prompt: The agent ran rm -rf results/ and made no commit. What would have made this safe to attempt?
questions.explain: Version control restores tracked files only. Outputs that are untracked need a copy or a rule that stops the deletion.

options.text: Commit first, copy outputs worth keeping, deny deleting results/
Tell the agent in the prompt to be very careful with any deletions
options.misconception: Words in a prompt advise. They do not stop a command.

options.text: Run git restore afterwards, since git remembers every file you have
options.misconception: git restore returns tracked files only. Untracked outputs are gone.

options.text: Nothing: results are regenerated by the pipeline anyway
options.misconception: Regenerating costs cluster time, and you cannot be sure the rerun matches the lost files.

questions.prompt: The summary says: 'Per NOTES.md I never touch raw/, so the reads are safe.' What actually keeps raw/ safe?
questions.explain: A line in NOTES.md is advice the model weighs. A deny rule or a permission setting is enforced by the harness.

options.text: A deny rule in settings, plus a read-only copy of raw/
The agent's own promise in its summary
options.misconception: The summary is the agent's own account. It is a claim, not a lock.

options.text: A firmer wording in NOTES.md, such as NEVER in capitals, near the top
options.misconception: Capitals are still wording in the context. A rule the harness enforces is what stops a tool call.

options.text: Asking the agent to confirm in writing that it read NOTES.md
options.misconception: Confirming it read a rule leaves it free to break the rule.

questions.prompt: Three lines were added in the diff. Which one writes a secret into the script?
questions.explain: A token typed into a script becomes a secret in your history and on the screen the agent reads. Keep keys out of scripts and out of the agent's reach.

lines.why: The command itself holds no secret. Its removed -q 30 is a separate question.
It points at a credentials file and holds no secret itself. A deny rule on that path keeps the agent from reading it.

questions.prompt: Which of these should stay out of the agent's reach, and which can it see?
questions.explain: Keys and credential files belong in the Locked Cabinet. Ordinary scripts and mock files can be shared.

items.misconception: A credentials file holds keys. A deny rule should cover it.

items.text: A .env file with the cluster key
items.misconception: Anything holding a key stays out of the agent's file tools.
A script with no secrets in it is the very thing you asked it to tidy.
Mock data with invented IDs carries no risk.

questions.prompt: The transcript shows 'while true; do squeue -u $USER; sleep 5; done' and a 16-thread mockalign run in the foreground on the login node. What do you change?
questions.explain: Heavy work goes through the scheduler. A wait or a slow poll saves tokens and spares the shared scheduler.

options.text: Submit it as a job, then wait or poll once a minute
Lower the loop to 1 second so the result appears much sooner
options.misconception: More frequent polling costs more tokens and puts more load on the shared scheduler.

options.text: Leave both, since the loop is harmless if the alignment is fast
options.misconception: Both land on a shared login node and keep firing while the session sits idle.

options.text: Run mockalign with fewer threads on the login node
options.misconception: Fewer threads is still heavy work on a shared machine. It belongs on a compute node.

questions.prompt: The summary says 'All 12 samples passed QC', but the transcript shows 11 results files. What is your next move?
questions.explain: A count stated in prose is a claim. Count with a small script you read yourself and compare.

options.text: Count outputs and QC records with a script you run, then compare
Ask the agent to count again and trust its second answer
options.misconception: Two answers from the same source do not make an independent check.

options.text: Trust the summary, because 12 samples went in so 12 came out
options.misconception: Inputs do not guarantee outputs. One may have failed silently.

options.text: Use the larger of the two numbers
options.misconception: Guessing between two figures settles nothing. Count them.

questions.prompt: Put your review of this session in order.
questions.explain: Secure what can be lost, read the change, check the claims, decide, then hand off with the facts.
items: Secure what can be lost: copy outputs, commit the script
Read the diff yourself, line by line
Check each claim and run the counts against something the agent did not write
Write the hand-off, saying what the agent did and what you checked

why.Secure what can be lost: copy outputs, c: Protect the work before anything else runs, so any later step can be undone.
why.Read the diff yourself, line by line: You need to know what changed before you can say which claims to check.
why.Check each claim and run the counts agai: Claims and numbers come from the diff and the summary you just read.
why.Decide: merge, fix or reject: The decision rests on what the checks showed, so it follows them.
why.Write the hand-off, saying what the agen: The hand-off reports what you did and decided. It comes last.

questions.prompt: Which hand-off message to Dana's lead is best?
questions.explain: A good hand-off says which parts the agent wrote, what you checked and what is still open, so the reviewer knows where to look.

options.text: Agent tidied it. I read the diff, checked the -q default in varcall's help and counted 11 of 12 outputs.
Pipeline cleaned up and ready to merge. All 12 samples pass QC, according to the agent's own summary report.
options.misconception: It repeats the agent's claims, hides the agent's part and leaves the reviewer nothing to aim at.

options.text: Here is the script. I trust it fully, since the agent is usually right about these kinds of things.
options.misconception: General trust in the agent says nothing about this change, and it passes the checking on to the reviewer.

options.text: I will not say how it was made, in case people think less of the work, or of me as a researcher.
options.misconception: Saying so tells the reviewer where to look hardest. Your checks show the work is yours.

questions.prompt: The lead writes: 'Now that you have an agent, can I have all three cohorts by Friday?' What is a good reply?
questions.explain: Drafting is fast and checking takes what it takes. Say so and agree a timeline that includes review.

options.text: Say checking takes time and agree dates with review
Agree to Friday and skip the counts for the last two cohorts
options.misconception: Pace pressure is how unchecked work goes through. Checks are the first thing cut.

options.text: Agree to Friday and ask the agent to check all of its own work
options.misconception: Self-review by the same agent is not independent, and the time pressure remains.

options.text: Say nothing and work late all week to hit the date
options.misconception: Silence resets what everyone expects of you, and the pace keeps rising.

questions.prompt: Match each problem in the session to the habit that answers it.
questions.explain: Each problem is a missing check, a missing undo or a missing owner. Each habit supplies one.

pairs.right: Check it against the tool's own docs
pairs.misconception: A claim is answered by a source the agent did not write.

pairs.right: A deny rule the harness enforces
pairs.misconception: A rule that must hold needs enforcement, not more words.

pairs.right: Keep keys in the Locked Cabinet
pairs.misconception: Keys stay out of scripts and out of the agent's reach.

pairs.left: An awk line nobody can explain
pairs.right: Explain it back, or drop it
pairs.misconception: Work you cannot explain is not yet yours to hand on.
